cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of an option's historical volatility, measured across successive trading days, for a series of options with different expiration dates.
cards.explanation: A volatility smile uses forward-looking implied volatility backed out of traded prices, not backward-looking historical volatility, and it varies strike while holding maturity fixed.
cards.originalText: The plot of an option's historical volatility, measured across successive trading days, for a series of options with different expiration dates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.
cards.explanation: A volatility smile plots implied volatility on the vertical axis against strike on the horizontal axis, with maturity held fixed.
cards.originalText: The plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.

cards.subject: Market Risk

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given strike price, as a function of its time to maturity.
cards.explanation: Holding strike fixed and varying maturity gives the volatility term structure. The smile holds maturity fixed and varies strike.
cards.originalText: The plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given strike price, as a function of its time to maturity.

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The implied volatility shape consistent with the lognormal price distribution assumed by BSM is a flat, horizontal line, because a single constant volatility prices every strike correctly.
cards.explanation: BSM assumes constant volatility and a lognormal terminal price, so one volatility would price every strike correctly and the implied volatility curve would be horizontal. Any smile or skew is a departure from BSM.
cards.originalText: A flat, horizontal line, because a single constant volatility prices every strike correctly.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on implied volatility
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical, because put-call parity forces the dollar pricing error of the model to be the same for both options.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity holds for both model and market prices, so the dollar pricing error on the call equals that on the put. Since price is strictly increasing in volatility, the same volatility zeroes both errors.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities are identical, because put-call parity forces the dollar pricing error of the model to be the same for both options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on implied volatility
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities differ, because a put's payoff is bounded above while a call's payoff is unbounded.
cards.explanation: Payoff asymmetry affects the price levels of calls and puts, but put-call parity forces their implied volatilities to be equal at a common strike and maturity.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities differ, because a put's payoff is bounded above while a call's payoff is unbounded.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on implied volatility
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical only when both options are at the money.
cards.explanation: Equality of call and put implied volatilities at a common strike and maturity holds at every strike, not only at the money, which is why calls and puts share a single smile.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities are identical only when both options are at the money.
cards.correction: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical whether or not both options are at the money.

cards.explanation: Equality of call and put implied volatilities at a common strike and maturity holds at every strike, not only at the money, which is why calls and puts share a single smile.

cards.statement: Different implied volatilities for a European call and a European put at the same strike and maturity are a normal feature of the volatility surface.

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A platykurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis below 3, produces a symmetric smile.
cards.explanation: A platykurtic (light-tailed) implied log return distribution makes deep in- and out-of-the-money contracts cheap relative to BSM and produces a frown, not a smile.
cards.correction: A platykurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis below 3, produces a frown.

cards.loText: Compare smile shape to the implied distribution and to option pricing
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A leptokurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis above 3, produces an inverted smile, or frown.
cards.explanation: A leptokurtic (heavy-tailed) implied log return distribution makes deep in- and out-of-the-money contracts expensive relative to BSM and produces a smile, not a frown.
cards.correction: A leptokurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis above 3, produces a smile.

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A normal mixture implied log return distribution produces a frown, because mixing two normal distributions reduces kurtosis below 3.
cards.explanation: A normal mixture has kurtosis above 3, so it has heavy tails and produces a smile rather than a frown.

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A platykurtic implied log return distribution produces a frown, in which at-the-money options carry a higher implied volatility than both deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options.
cards.explanation: Light tails make deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money contracts worth less than BSM implies, depressing both wings and leaving the at-the-money implied volatility highest, which is a frown.

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: End users such as pension funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money put options for downside protection is likely to steepen the downward-sloping skew in equity index options.
cards.explanation: Out-of-the-money puts sit at low strikes, so extra demand for them raises low-strike implied volatility and steepens the downward skew. This is crashophobia expressed as order flow.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump; as option maturity increases, the volatility smile becomes less pronounced.
cards.explanation: Exchange rates violate both lognormality conditions (constant volatility and no jumps). Both effects matter less at longer maturities, so the FX smile becomes less pronounced as maturity increases.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump; as option maturity increases, the volatility smile becomes more pronounced.
cards.explanation: The FX smile becomes less, not more, pronounced as time to maturity increases.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Exchange rates satisfy the constant volatility condition but violate the smooth-diffusion condition; the effect of jumps on implied volatility is independent of maturity.
cards.explanation: Exchange rate volatility is not constant, so both lognormality conditions fail. The impact of jumps on implied volatility is strongly maturity dependent and diminishes as maturity lengthens.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump, but because both effects are strike-independent they shift the level of the curve without changing its shape.
cards.explanation: Non-constant volatility and jumps affect prices differently across strikes, which is exactly what creates the FX smile. A strike-independent effect would only shift the level of a flat curve.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe FX rate distributions and their implications
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Standard geometric Brownian motion is an adequate representation of the price process of a currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.
cards.explanation: A pegged currency is the archetypal jump process: it barely moves, then moves discontinuously when the peg is realigned or breaks. A pure diffusion such as GBM cannot generate that path.
cards.originalText: A currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.
cards.correction: Standard geometric Brownian motion is an inadequate representation of the price process of a currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.

cards.subject: Market Risk

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Standard geometric Brownian motion is an adequate representation of the price process of any currency, provided the modelling horizon is short.
cards.explanation: Jumps matter most at short horizons because there is less diffusion to dilute them. The impact of jumps dissipates at long horizons, so a short horizon makes GBM less adequate, not more.
cards.originalText: Any currency, provided the modelling horizon is short.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the equity and FX smiles and explain their shape
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The downward-sloping volatility skew in equity index options is explained by capital structure leverage, whereby a fall in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and by crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money puts because they fear a repeat of a market crash.
cards.explanation: Falling equity value raises leverage and hence equity volatility (a negative price-volatility relationship), and crash fear bids up out-of-the-money puts. Both lift implied volatility at low strikes.
cards.originalText: Capital structure leverage, whereby a fall in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money puts because they fear a repeat of a market crash.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the equity and FX smiles and explain their shape
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The downward-sloping volatility skew in equity index options is explained by capital structure leverage, whereby a rise in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and by crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money calls because they fear missing a rally.
cards.explanation: Leverage rises when equity value falls, not when it rises, and crashophobia concerns out-of-the-money puts bought as crash insurance, not calls.
cards.originalText: Capital structure leverage, whereby a rise in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money calls because they fear missing a rally.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and surfaces and their use in pricing
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A downward-sloping volatility term structure, with short-dated implied volatilities well above long-dated ones, is most plausibly explained by mean reversion in volatility.
cards.explanation: Mean-reverting volatility is pulled toward a long-run level, so when short-dated volatility is high it is expected to fall, producing a downward-sloping term structure.
cards.originalText: Mean reversion in volatility

cards.explanation: The GARCH(1,1) long-run variance is a fixed parameter that can sit above or below the current conditional variance.

cards.statement: GARCH(1,1) implies mean reversion in volatility, so the volatility term structure slopes upward or downward depending on whether current volatility is below or above the long-run level.

cards.explanation: Under GARCH(1,1), expected future variance depends strongly on current variance; the dependence decays as the horizon lengthens but does not vanish.

cards.correction: GARCH(1,1) implies a strong relationship between current volatility and expected future volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a smile
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: When a stock is expected to jump sharply either up or down on an imminent announcement, the short-dated implied volatility curve is a pronounced smile, because the anticipated jump fattens both tails of the distribution relative to lognormal.
cards.explanation: A single anticipated two-sided jump makes the distribution bimodal, emptying the middle rather than extending the extremes. The result is a frown, not a smile.
cards.originalText: A pronounced smile, because the anticipated jump fattens both tails of the distribution relative to lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a smile
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: When a stock is expected to jump sharply either up or down on an imminent announcement, the short-dated implied volatility curve is a frown, because the anticipated jump makes the distribution bimodal, so at-the-money options are expensive relative to a lognormal benchmark while deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options are cheap.
cards.explanation: A single anticipated two-sided jump concentrates probability at two points and hollows out the middle. At-the-money contracts become expensive and the wings cheap relative to lognormal, so the implied volatility curve frowns.
cards.originalText: A frown, because the anticipated jump makes the distribution bimodal, so at-the-money options are expensive relative to a lognormal benchmark while deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options are cheap.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the sum of two components, current VaR plus stressed VaR, whereas the FRTB requires only a single stressed expected shortfall.
cards.explanation: Basel II.5 summed current VaR and stressed VaR; the FRTB collapses this into a single expected shortfall calibrated to a 12-month stressed period.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel I and II.5 calculated market risk capital using a single 10-day horizon, whereas the FRTB uses five different liquidity horizons depending on the liquidity of the market variable.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the fixed 10-day horizon with five liquidity horizons assigned according to the liquidity of each risk factor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the default risk charge, which the FRTB eliminates, so that total market risk capital requirements are expected to fall.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge with a default risk charge rather than eliminating default risk capital, and total market risk capital is expected to rise rather than fall.
cards.correction: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the incremental risk charge, which the FRTB replaces, and total market risk capital requirements are expected to rise.

cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the incremental risk charge, which the FRTB replaces, and total market risk capital requirements are expected to rise.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge with a default risk charge rather than eliminating default risk capital, and total market risk capital is expected to rise rather than fall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel I and II.5 calculated the requirement from VaR at a 99.0% confidence level, whereas the FRTB calculates it from expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level.
cards.explanation: The FRTB moves the internal models measure from 99% VaR to 97.5% expected shortfall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations | Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The major motivation behind the FRTB's changes to the treatment of the trading book relative to the banking book is regulatory arbitrage between the two books.
cards.explanation: Pre-FRTB, the same economic exposure could attract a lower capital charge in one book than the other, so banks could choose their charge by choosing the book. The FRTB boundary rules aim to close that gap.
cards.originalText: Regulatory arbitrage between the two books

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 99% confidence level, which is materially more conservative for every distribution.
cards.explanation: The FRTB uses expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, not 99%, and it is not more conservative for every distribution; under normality it is almost equivalent to 99% VaR.
cards.correction: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, which can be materially more conservative for a heavier-tailed distribution.

cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, which can be materially more conservative for a heavier-tailed distribution.
cards.explanation: The FRTB uses expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, not 99%, and it is not more conservative for every distribution; under normality it is almost equivalent to 99% VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level. For a normal distribution the two are almost exactly equivalent, but for a heavier-tailed distribution the 97.5% expected shortfall can be much greater than the 99% VaR.
cards.explanation: Under normality, 99% VaR is about 2.326 standard deviations and 97.5% ES about 2.338, so the switch is close to capital neutral. With heavier tails, the tail average can far exceed the quantile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, which is necessarily lower than 99% VaR because the confidence level has been reduced.
cards.explanation: The lower confidence level is offset by moving from a quantile to a tail average; under normality 97.5% ES is almost exactly equal to 99% VaR, and with heavy tails it can be much larger.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB retains 99% VaR but requires it to be calculated over a stressed period rather than a current period.
cards.explanation: The FRTB does not retain VaR as the capital measure; it uses stressed expected shortfall at 97.5%. VaR survives only in backtesting.

cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under Basel II.5, stressed VaR is calibrated to a 250-day period of stressed market conditions.
cards.explanation: Stressed VaR under Basel II.5 is calculated from a 250-day (roughly one trading year) period of stressed market conditions; the FRTB carries this forward as a 12-month stressed period.
cards.originalText: A 250-day period

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A risk charge calculated under the sensitivities-based method is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The FRTB standardised approach is the simple sum of the sensitivities-based method charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on.
cards.originalText: A risk charge calculated under the sensitivities-based method

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A residual risk add-on is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The residual risk add-on is one of the three components and captures exotic underlyings and residual risks the other components do not reach.
cards.originalText: A residual risk add-on

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A default risk charge is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The default risk charge is one of the three components and is the FRTB successor to the incremental risk charge.
cards.originalText: A default risk charge

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: An incremental risk charge is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The incremental risk charge is the Basel II.5 measure that the FRTB replaced with the default risk charge. The three components are the sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on.
cards.originalText: An incremental risk charge

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Credit spread risk, securitisation (correlation trading portfolio) is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: Credit spread risk is split into three classes: non-securitisation, securitisation outside the correlation trading portfolio, and securitisation within it.
cards.originalText: Credit spread risk, securitisation (correlation trading portfolio)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Funding liquidity risk is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: Funding liquidity risk is governed by the LCR and NSFR, outside the market risk capital framework. The seven classes cover interest rate, three credit spread classes, equity, commodity and FX risk.
cards.originalText: Funding liquidity risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: General interest rate risk is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: General interest rate risk is the first of the seven sensitivities-based risk classes.
cards.originalText: General interest rate risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Commodity risk is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: Commodity risk is one of the seven sensitivities-based risk classes.
cards.originalText: Commodity risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The simplified standardised approach proposed by the Basel Committee in June 2017 is intended for global systemically important banks with large and complex trading operations.
cards.explanation: Global systemically important banks with large trading operations are exactly the institutions for which the simplified approach is inadequate. It is intended for banks with low trading book activity or limited infrastructure.
cards.originalText: Global systemically important banks with large and complex trading operations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The simplified standardised approach proposed by the Basel Committee in June 2017 is intended for banks whose trading desks have failed the backtesting exception thresholds.
cards.explanation: A desk that fails backtesting is moved to the full standardised approach as a sanction. The simplified standardised approach is a concession for small or unsophisticated banks, not a penalty.
cards.originalText: Banks whose trading desks have failed the backtesting exception thresholds.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The simplified standardised approach proposed by the Basel Committee in June 2017 is intended for banks with a low concentration of trading book activity, or that lack the infrastructure to implement the sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: The simplified standardised approach is a proportionality concession for small or unsophisticated banks, for which the full sensitivities-based method would be disproportionately costly.
cards.originalText: Banks with a low concentration of trading book activity, or that lack the infrastructure to implement the sensitivities-based method.
