cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the standardised approach, the capital requirement is the sum of three components: a sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge, and the residual risk add-on.
cards.explanation: The FRTB standardised approach requirement is the simple sum of the sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations | Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the internal models approach, the fixed 10-day liquidity horizon of Basel 2.5 is replaced by asset-class specific liquidity horizons of up to 120 days.
cards.explanation: The single 10-day horizon is replaced by five liquidity horizons running from 10 up to 120 days under the final standard.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations | Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the internal models approach, the 99.0% VaR of Basel 2.5, both current and stressed, is replaced by a 97.5% stressed expected shortfall.
cards.explanation: The headline change in the internal models risk measure is from 99% VaR (current plus stressed) to 97.5% stressed expected shortfall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Describe the FRTB changes to market risk capital and the motivations | Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under neither approach does the FRTB impose charges for credit-related exposures such as credit spread risk or jump-to-default risk, because those exposures are capitalised under the credit risk framework instead.
cards.explanation: The FRTB explicitly capitalises credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk within the market risk framework under both approaches, for example through the credit spread risk classes and the default risk charge.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to market risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and are subject to credit risk capital.
cards.explanation: Trading book positions are held with intent to trade, marked to market daily and attract market risk capital; banking book positions are expected to be held to maturity, are not marked to market daily and attract credit risk capital.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to credit risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and are subject to market risk capital.
cards.explanation: The capital regimes are the other way round: trading book instruments attract market risk capital and banking book instruments attract credit risk capital.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Instruments in both books are marked to market daily under the FRTB, but only trading book instruments attract market risk capital.
cards.explanation: The FRTB did not extend daily mark to market to the banking book; banking book instruments are carried at amortised or historical cost, which is why the boundary matters.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Trading book instruments are valued at historical cost and are subject to market risk capital; banking book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to liquidity risk capital.
cards.explanation: Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and attract market risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and attract credit risk capital. There is no liquidity risk capital charge in this framework.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB collapses the banking book and the trading book into a single book, which removes the arbitrage opportunity entirely.
cards.explanation: The banking book and trading book remain distinct under the FRTB, attracting credit risk and market risk capital respectively. The FRTB instead makes the boundary more objective and limits movement between books.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB makes no change to the boundary but subjects both books to identical capital calculations.
cards.explanation: The FRTB substantially changes the boundary, making it more objective and restricting movement between books, and the two books are not subject to identical capital calculations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB retains a subjective intent-to-trade test as the necessary and sufficient condition for trading book inclusion, and imposes the incremental risk charge as a penalty when a position is moved between books.
cards.explanation: The FRTB moves away from a purely subjective intent-to-trade test toward objective criteria. The incremental risk charge was a Basel II.5 charge for credit-dependent trading book instruments, not a reclassification penalty.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB establishes a more objective boundary, including assignment at the point a position is initiated and strict limits on subsequent movement between the books.
cards.explanation: The FRTB closes the arbitrage by making the boundary objective (presumptive lists and evidence-based criteria), assigning positions at initiation, and strictly limiting subsequent reclassification.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, the backtesting methodology is unchanged from the earlier regime.
cards.explanation: FRTB backtesting changes from a single 99% one-day VaR test to tests at both 97.5% and 99%, applied at desk level with hard consequences.
cards.originalText: The backtesting methodology is unchanged under the FRTB.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, a one-day static VaR, calibrated to the most recent 12 months of data, is backtested at both the 97.5th and the 99th percentiles, at the level of each individual trading desk.
cards.explanation: The FRTB backtest uses one-day VaR on current (12-month) data, at both the 97.5% and 99% levels, applied to each trading desk, with hard consequences for breaches.
cards.originalText: A one-day static VaR, calibrated to the most recent 12 months of data, is backtested at BOTH the 97.5th and the 99th percentiles, at the level of each individual trading desk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, there are two backtests: a 10-day 99.0% expected shortfall and a 10-day 99.0% stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: FRTB backtesting uses one-day VaR at 97.5% and 99%. Neither expected shortfall nor a stressed measure is backtested.
cards.originalText: There are two tests: a 10-day 99.0% expected shortfall and a 10-day 99.0% stressed VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, the backtesting horizon of 10 days and the 99.0% confidence level are unchanged, but they are now applied to expected shortfall rather than to VaR.
cards.explanation: The FRTB backtest horizon is one day, not 10, and the backtested measure is VaR, not expected shortfall.
cards.originalText: The 10-day horizon and the 99.0% confidence level are unchanged, but they are now applied to expected shortfall rather than to VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is not a coherent risk measure and so cannot be validated statistically.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure, which is one reason the FRTB adopted it. Coherence is unrelated to backtestability.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB backtests one-day VaR on recent data rather than the expected shortfall used for capital because backtesting a 10-day expected shortfall is difficult, and backtesting a stressed measure is in theory impossible, so a measure calibrated to current data is required.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall is a tail average with no threshold to breach, so it is hard to backtest, and a stressed measure calibrated to a historical stress window cannot be compared with current outcomes at all. The FRTB therefore backtests one-day VaR on current data.
cards.originalText: Backtesting a 10-day expected shortfall is difficult, and backtesting a STRESSED measure is in theory impossible, so a measure calibrated to current data is required.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Regulators require the backtest measure to match the measure used for the standardised approach, which is based on VaR.
cards.explanation: The FRTB standardised approach is not based on VaR; it is the sum of a sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on. Backtesting applies only to internal models.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, when a trading desk breaches the backtesting exception thresholds, all positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach, until the desk no longer exceeds the thresholds over the prior 12 months.
cards.explanation: A desk with more than 12 exceptions at the 99th percentile or more than 30 at the 97.5th in the most recent 12 months must capitalise all its positions under the standardised approach. The consequence is desk level and reversible once the desk is back within the thresholds.
cards.originalText: All positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach, until the desk no longer exceeds the thresholds over the prior 12 months.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, when a trading desk breaches the backtesting exception thresholds, all positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach permanently, because internal models approval once withdrawn cannot be regained.
cards.explanation: The exclusion is not permanent: a desk returns to the internal models approach once it is back within both exception thresholds over the prior 12 months.
cards.originalText: All positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach permanently, because internal models approval once withdrawn cannot be regained.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB makes no change to the incremental risk charge.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with the default risk charge, which recognises jump-to-default risk and includes equity products.
cards.correction: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with the default risk charge, which recognises jump-to-default risk and includes equity products.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which recognises jump-to-default risk and mandates the inclusion of equity products.
cards.explanation: The FRTB separates credit spread risk (handled inside expected shortfall) from jump-to-default risk, and the default risk charge that replaces the IRC captures jump-to-default and extends to equity products.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from downgrade risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which explicitly excludes equity products.
cards.explanation: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, not downgrade risk (migration is captured within credit spread risk), and the default risk charge includes equity products rather than excluding them.
cards.correction: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which explicitly includes equity products.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which explicitly includes equity products.
cards.explanation: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, not downgrade risk (migration is captured within credit spread risk), and the default risk charge includes equity products rather than excluding them.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB retains the IRC but recalibrates it to a 10-day, 97.5% confidence expected shortfall, consistent with the market risk measure.
cards.explanation: The IRC is not retained; it is replaced by the default risk charge. Jump-to-default keeps a banking-book-style calibration of one year at 99.9%, not the 10-day 97.5% market risk parameters.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures may be capitalised under the internal models approach provided the bank's model has been approved for the correlation trading portfolio.
cards.explanation: Under the FRTB, all securitisation exposures, including the correlation trading portfolio, must be capitalised under the standardised approach; internal models are not available for them.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures may be capitalised under the internal models approach, but with a liquidity horizon floor of 120 days.
cards.explanation: There is no internal models route for securitisations under the FRTB; they must use the standardised approach.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures are exempt from market risk capital and attract credit risk capital in the banking book instead.
cards.explanation: Securitisation exposures held with trading intent remain in the trading book and attract market risk capital. The FRTB removes the choice of approach, requiring the standardised approach, not the applicability of the market risk framework.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: FRTB Book Boundary and Model Tests
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions: book boundary, backtesting, PLA, credit, securitizations
cards.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures must be capitalised under the STANDARDISED approach, because the internal models banks developed for these exposures under the earlier comprehensive risk measure differed widely from one another.
cards.explanation: Under the earlier comprehensive risk measure, banks' own models for securitisations differed widely, so similar exposures attracted very different capital. The FRTB therefore mandates the standardised approach for securitisations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Negative rates are attractive to lenders because they eliminate lending risk.
cards.explanation: A negative rate means the lender is repaid less than was lent, which makes lending unattractive. The rate paid is also unrelated to credit risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Negative short-term rates affect neither borrowers nor lenders, because rates revert to positive levels in the long run.
cards.explanation: Negative rates today affect borrowing and lending decisions today, regardless of where rates settle later, and a Gaussian model assigns positive probability to negative rates at every horizon.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Negative rates cannot arise in practice because central banks are legally prohibited from setting a policy rate below zero.
cards.explanation: There is no legal prohibition on negative policy rates, and several major central banks have set them. The lower bound on rates is economic and approximate, not legal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Individuals will generally not lend at a negative rate, because they can instead hold cash and earn zero.
cards.explanation: Physical cash is a zero-yield alternative, so lending at a negative rate is dominated by holding cash. This creates the zero lower bound, which in practice sits slightly below zero because holding cash has storage and insurance costs.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: When negative rates in an interest rate tree are set to zero, the rates in the original tree are the observed rates and the rates in the adjusted tree are the shadow rates.
cards.explanation: The labels are reversed: the original, unadjusted rates are the shadow rates, and the adjusted, floored rates are the observed rates.
cards.originalText: Original rates are the observed rates; adjusted rates are the shadow rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: When negative rates in an interest rate tree are set to zero, the rates in the original tree are the shadow rates and the rates in the adjusted tree are the observed rates.
cards.explanation: When a tree is built from the chosen distribution and negative nodes are set to zero, the unadjusted rates are shadow rates (hypothetical, possibly negative) and the floored rates are the observed, transactable rates used for discounting.
cards.originalText: Original rates are the shadow rates; adjusted rates are the observed rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Flooring a normally distributed tree at zero leaves the mean and volatility of the modelled rate unchanged, which is why it is preferred to changing the distribution.
cards.explanation: Truncating the left tail of a normally distributed tree at zero raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate. That distortion is the drawback of the flooring approach.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The only available method for preventing negative short-term rates in a term structure model is to adopt a distribution that cannot go negative, such as a lognormal or square-root process, because flooring a tree introduces arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Flooring a tree at zero is a recognised method alongside changing the distribution, and it does not introduce arbitrage; its cost is that it distorts the distribution.
cards.originalText: The only available method is to adopt a distribution that cannot go negative, such as a lognormal or square-root process, because flooring a tree introduces arbitrage.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: There are two methods for preventing negative short-term rates in a term structure model: flooring a normally distributed tree at zero, and adopting a distribution that cannot produce negative rates. Flooring raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate relative to the unadjusted model.
cards.explanation: Negative rates can be prevented either by flooring a tree at zero or by using a process that cannot go negative, such as lognormal or square-root. Truncating the left tail raises the mean and lowers the volatility.
cards.originalText: There are two methods: flooring a normally distributed tree at zero, and adopting a distribution that cannot produce negative rates. Flooring raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate relative to the unadjusted model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing negative short-term rates
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: Methods for preventing negative short-term rates in term structure models are unnecessary in practice, since observed nominal short rates have never been negative.
cards.explanation: Negative nominal policy and market rates have been observed in Japan, Switzerland and the euro area, which is why preventing or handling negative rates matters in practice.
cards.originalText: There are two methods, but both are unnecessary in practice, since observed nominal short rates have never been negative.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The principal use of an arbitrage-free term structure model is determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.
cards.explanation: An arbitrage-free model takes market prices as inputs, so it cannot judge whether they are fair. Assessing fair value calls for an equilibrium model.
cards.originalText: Determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.
cards.correction: The principal use of an equilibrium term structure model is determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The principal use of an equilibrium term structure model is determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.
cards.explanation: An arbitrage-free model takes market prices as inputs, so it cannot judge whether they are fair. Assessing fair value calls for an equilibrium model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The principal use of an arbitrage-free term structure model is forecasting the level of the short-term rate over long horizons.
cards.explanation: The drift in an arbitrage-free model is a risk-neutral calibration parameter that bundles expectations with a risk premium, so it is not a real-world forecast of rates.
cards.originalText: Forecasting the level of the short-term rate over long horizons.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The principal use of an arbitrage-free term structure model is quoting the prices of securities that are not actively traded, on the basis of the prices of more liquid securities.
cards.explanation: An arbitrage-free model is calibrated to reproduce the prices of liquid securities exactly, so it is suited to pricing illiquid securities consistently with the liquid instruments used to hedge them.
cards.originalText: Quoting the prices of securities that are not actively traded, on the basis of the prices of more liquid securities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: An exact fit of an arbitrage-free term structure model to market prices guarantees that the model will continue to price accurately as the term structure moves, because the calibration is re-derived at every node.
cards.explanation: Fitting today's prices says nothing about tomorrow's. Arbitrage-free models generally need recalibration as the curve moves, and frequent large refits indicate instability.
cards.originalText: An exact fit guarantees that the model will continue to price accurately as the term structure moves, because the calibration is re-derived at every node.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe uses of arbitrage-free models and assess fitting to market prices
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: An exact fit of an arbitrage-free term structure model to observed bond prices means the model takes market prices as correct, so it cannot identify mispricing; and if the fit requires an implausible path for the drift, that is evidence that either the model or some of the fitted prices should be questioned.
cards.explanation: A model calibrated to reproduce prices exactly absorbs any mispricing into its drift, so it cannot say the market is wrong. If the calibrated drift path looks implausible, the model or some fitted prices deserve scrutiny.
cards.originalText: An exact fit means the model takes market prices as correct, so it cannot identify mispricing; and if the fit requires an implausible path for the drift, that is evidence that either the model or some of the fitted prices should be questioned.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In a short-rate model with a time-dependent volatility function sigma(t), the volatility of the short rate depends on the level of the short rate itself.
cards.explanation: When volatility is a function of time alone, the rate does not appear in the diffusion term. Volatility depending on the rate level is a different specification, such as square-root or lognormal processes.
cards.originalText: On the level of the short rate itself.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In a short-rate model with a time-dependent volatility function sigma(t), the volatility of the short rate depends on time.
cards.explanation: A volatility function of time alone has calendar time as its only argument, so the short-rate volatility is a deterministic function of calendar time.
cards.originalText: On time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: At expiration, a caplet pays the difference between the short rate and the strike rate, if that difference is positive, on a notional amount.
cards.explanation: A caplet is a call on an interest rate: it pays notional times the positive part of the rate minus the strike (times the day count fraction), insuring against rising rates.
cards.originalText: The difference between the short rate and the strike rate, if that difference is positive, on a notional amount.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: At expiration, a caplet pays the difference between the short rate and the strike rate, if that difference is negative, on a notional amount.
cards.explanation: A caplet pays when the rate exceeds the strike. Paying when the rate is below the strike describes a floorlet, which insures against falling rates.
cards.originalText: The difference between the short rate and the strike rate, if that difference is negative, on a notional amount.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: At expiration, a caplet pays the short rate on a notional amount, regardless of the strike rate.
cards.explanation: A caplet pays only the positive excess of the short rate over the strike on the notional. A payment of the short rate regardless of the strike would be an unconditional floating payment with no optionality.
cards.originalText: The short rate on a notional amount, regardless of the strike rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In Model 3, where short-rate volatility equals sigma times exp(-alpha t) with positive alpha, volatility begins at the constant sigma and decays exponentially towards zero.
cards.explanation: In Model 3 the volatility term is sigma times exp(-alpha t). At time zero this equals sigma, and as time passes the exponential factor decays toward zero at speed alpha.
cards.originalText: Volatility begins at the constant sigma and decays exponentially towards zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In Model 3, where short-rate volatility equals sigma times exp(-alpha t) with positive alpha, volatility begins at the constant sigma and grows exponentially without bound.
cards.explanation: With a negative exponent, exp(-alpha t) falls over time, so Model 3 volatility starts at sigma and decays toward zero rather than growing.
cards.originalText: Volatility begins at the constant sigma and grows exponentially without bound.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under time-dependent volatility
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: In Model 3, where short-rate volatility equals sigma times exp(-alpha t) with positive alpha, volatility begins at zero and rises exponentially towards the constant sigma.
cards.explanation: Model 3 volatility starts at sigma (since exp(0) equals one) and falls toward zero; it does not start at zero and rise.
cards.originalText: Volatility begins at zero and rises exponentially towards the constant sigma.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Assess the efficacy of time-dependent volatility models
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: To price a fixed income option, a model with time-dependent volatility is preferable; to price and hedge fixed income securities, a model with mean reversion is preferable.
cards.explanation: A time-dependent volatility function can match a strip of quoted cap or swaption prices exactly, which suits pricing and interpolating such derivatives. Mean reversion produces a realistic volatility term structure and co-movement across maturities, which hedge ratios depend on.
cards.originalText: Time-dependent volatility for the option; mean reversion for the securities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Assess the efficacy of time-dependent volatility models
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: To price a fixed income option, a model with mean reversion is preferable; to price and hedge fixed income securities, a model with time-dependent volatility is preferable.
cards.explanation: The pairing is the other way round: time-dependent volatility suits pricing fixed income derivatives such as caps, and mean reversion suits pricing and hedging fixed income securities.
cards.originalText: Mean reversion for the option; time-dependent volatility for the securities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Assess the efficacy of time-dependent volatility models
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The objection that time-dependent volatility models imply a specific forecast of short-rate volatility in the distant future is addressed by assuming volatility depends on time in the near term and then settles at a constant thereafter.
cards.explanation: The market may plausibly have a view on volatility over the next year or two, where traded derivative prices carry information, but not decades out. Holding volatility constant beyond the near term avoids asserting a precise distant-future forecast.
cards.originalText: Assume volatility depends on time in the near term and then settles at a constant thereafter.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Assess the efficacy of time-dependent volatility models
cards.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
cards.statement: The objection that time-dependent volatility models imply a specific forecast of short-rate volatility in the distant future is addressed by assuming volatility depends on time in the near term and then decays without limit.
cards.explanation: Unlimited decay is the original problem: a model such as Model 3 drives volatility to zero in the far future, which practitioners object to. The remedy is to hold volatility constant beyond the near term.
cards.originalText: Assume volatility depends on time in the near term and then decays without limit.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: The institution selling a quanto option does not know in advance the amount of foreign currency that will need to be converted, nor the exchange rate at maturity at which the conversion would otherwise have taken place.
cards.explanation: The seller of a quanto does not know how much foreign currency the payoff will require, nor the exchange rate at which it would otherwise be converted at maturity. The interaction of these two unknowns is what makes the quanto a correlation product.
cards.originalText: The amount of foreign currency that will need to be converted, and the exchange rate at maturity at which the conversion would otherwise have taken place.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: The institution selling a quanto option does not know in advance the strike price of the option or the volatility of the underlying at maturity.
cards.explanation: The strike of a quanto is contractually fixed at inception. The seller's quanto-specific unknowns are the amount of foreign currency to be converted and the exchange rate at maturity.
cards.originalText: The strike price of the option, and the volatility of the underlying at maturity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: The value of a quanto call is unaffected by the correlation between the foreign asset and the exchange rate, because the conversion rate is fixed.
cards.explanation: Fixing the conversion rate is what creates the correlation exposure. The correlation enters the quanto drift with a negative sign, so it does affect the value.
cards.originalText: The value of the quanto call is unaffected, because the conversion rate is fixed.
cards.correction: The value of a quanto call is affected by the correlation between the foreign asset and the exchange rate, because the conversion rate is fixed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: The value of a quanto call is affected by the correlation between the foreign asset and the exchange rate, because the conversion rate is fixed.
cards.explanation: Fixing the conversion rate is what creates the correlation exposure. The correlation enters the quanto drift with a negative sign, so it does affect the value.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: For a quanto call on a foreign equity index, an increase in the correlation between the index and the exchange rate (units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency) lowers the value of the call, all else equal.
cards.explanation: The quanto drift equals the foreign rate minus the yield minus the correlation times the two volatilities. A higher correlation lowers the drift of the foreign asset and so lowers the value of a quanto call.
cards.originalText: The value of the quanto call falls.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: An increase in the correlation between two assets raises the value of both an exchange option and a basket call on them, because higher correlation raises the volatility of any multi-asset payoff.
cards.explanation: Higher correlation raises the volatility of a sum but lowers the volatility of a difference, so a contract paying the difference falls in value while a basket call rises.
cards.originalText: Both values rise, because higher correlation raises the volatility of any multi-asset payoff.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: An increase in the correlation between two assets lowers the value of an exchange option on them and raises the value of a basket call on their equally weighted average.
cards.explanation: Higher correlation lowers the volatility of a difference of two assets and raises the volatility of their sum, so a contract paying the difference loses value and a basket call gains.
cards.originalText: The exchange option falls in value and the basket call rises.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts quanto and other multi-asset exotic option prices
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: An increase in the correlation between two assets raises the value of an exchange option on them and lowers the value of a basket call on their equally weighted average.
cards.explanation: The effects are the other way round: a contract paying the difference of two assets depends on the volatility of a difference, which falls with correlation, while a basket call depends on the volatility of a sum, which rises.
cards.originalText: The exchange option rises in value and the basket call falls.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses and payoffs of a correlation swap
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: A correlation swap is an exchange-traded contract in which the buyer receives a payoff only if realised correlation exceeds the fixed rate, making it an option on correlation.
cards.explanation: Correlation swaps trade over the counter, and the payoff is symmetric, so the buyer pays when realised correlation falls below the fixed rate. A one-sided payoff would make it a call on correlation requiring an upfront premium.
cards.originalText: An exchange-traded contract in which the buyer receives a payoff only if realised correlation exceeds the fixed rate, making it an option on correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses and payoffs of a correlation swap
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: A correlation swap is a contract whose payoff depends on the correlation between an equity index and its own implied volatility, used principally to hedge quanto exposures.
cards.explanation: A correlation swap references the realised average pairwise correlation of a basket of assets. Quanto exposures involve the correlation between an asset and an exchange rate, which is a different quantity.
cards.originalText: A contract whose payoff depends on the correlation between an equity index and its own implied volatility, used principally to hedge quanto exposures.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses and payoffs of a correlation swap
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: A correlation swap is an over-the-counter contract in which both parties exchange the realised variances of the individual assets in a basket, used to hedge dispersion risk.
cards.explanation: Exchanging index variance against single-name variances describes a dispersion trade. A correlation swap settles directly on realised average pairwise correlation versus a fixed rate.
cards.originalText: An over-the-counter contract in which both parties exchange the realised variances of the individual assets in a basket, used to hedge dispersion risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses and payoffs of a correlation swap
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: A correlation swap is an over-the-counter contract in which the buyer of correlation pays a fixed correlation rate and receives the realised average pairwise correlation of a basket on a notional, used to take a directional view on correlation or to hedge an existing short-correlation exposure.
cards.explanation: A correlation swap is traded over the counter with a linear, symmetric payoff of notional times realised minus fixed correlation. It is used for directional correlation views and to hedge short-correlation books.
cards.originalText: An over-the-counter contract in which the buyer of correlation pays a fixed correlation rate and receives the realised average pairwise correlation of a basket on a notional, used to take a directional view on correlation or to hedge an existing short-correlation exposure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Systemic risk and correlation risk are largely independent of one another.
cards.explanation: Systemic risk and correlation risk are highly dependent: correlations across almost all risky asset classes rose toward one during the 2007 to 2009 crisis.
cards.originalText: They are largely independent of one another.
cards.correction: Systemic risk and correlation risk are highly dependent on one another.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Systemic risk and correlation risk are highly dependent on one another.
cards.explanation: Systemic risk and correlation risk are highly dependent: correlations across almost all risky asset classes rose toward one during the 2007 to 2009 crisis.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Systemic risk and correlation risk are highly dependent, because a systemic event causes correlations across asset classes to rise sharply and simultaneously.
cards.explanation: In a crisis investors sell whatever is liquid, so assets with no fundamental link fall together and correlations converge toward one. Conversely, correlation changes break hedges and models calibrated to normal periods, causing systemic losses.
cards.originalText: They are highly dependent, because a systemic event causes correlations across asset classes to rise sharply and simultaneously.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Systemic risk and correlation risk are inversely related, because diversification across institutions reduces systemic risk.
cards.explanation: Diversification within a portfolio reduces that portfolio's risk, but when all institutions hold similar diversified portfolios systemic risk increases. Systemic risk and correlation risk move together, not inversely.
cards.originalText: They are inversely related, because diversification across institutions reduces systemic risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: For a creditor, the LOWER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the LOWER the overall portfolio default risk.
cards.explanation: With n equal-sized loans the concentration ratio is 1/n, so more borrowers means a lower ratio, more diversification and lower portfolio default risk.
cards.originalText: The LOWER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the LOWER the overall portfolio default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: For a creditor, the HIGHER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the LOWER the overall portfolio default risk.
cards.explanation: A higher concentration ratio means fewer effective borrowers and therefore less diversification and higher portfolio default risk.
cards.originalText: The HIGHER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the LOWER the overall portfolio default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: For a creditor, the LOWER the concentration ratio, the LOWER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.
cards.explanation: A lower concentration ratio means more borrowers, so diversification is higher and overall portfolio default risk is lower.
cards.originalText: The LOWER the concentration ratio, the LOWER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: For a creditor, the HIGHER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.
cards.explanation: A higher concentration ratio means less diversification, not more. A lower concentration ratio corresponds to higher diversification and lower portfolio default risk.
cards.originalText: The HIGHER the concentration ratio, the HIGHER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.
cards.correction: For a creditor, the HIGHER the concentration ratio, the LOWER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: For a creditor, the HIGHER the concentration ratio, the LOWER the diversification, and the HIGHER the overall portfolio default risk.
cards.explanation: A higher concentration ratio means less diversification, not more. A lower concentration ratio corresponds to higher diversification and lower portfolio default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Intersector default correlations are typically HIGHER than intrasector correlations, so a lender seeking to reduce default correlation should specialise in a single sector.
cards.explanation: Intersector default correlations are typically lower than intrasector correlations, so reducing default correlation calls for diversifying across sectors rather than specialising.
cards.originalText: Intersector default correlations are typically HIGHER than intrasector correlations, so the lender should specialise in a single sector.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Intrasector default correlations are typically HIGHER than intersector correlations, so a lender seeking to reduce default correlation should build a sector-diversified loan portfolio.
cards.explanation: Firms in the same sector share customers, costs, regulation and demand, so their defaults are more correlated than those of firms in different sectors. Diversifying across sectors therefore reduces portfolio default correlation.
cards.originalText: Intrasector default correlations are typically HIGHER than intersector correlations, so the lender should build a sector-diversified loan portfolio.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Intrasector default correlations are typically LOWER than intersector correlations, so a lender seeking to reduce default correlation should specialise in a single sector.
cards.explanation: Intrasector default correlations are typically higher than intersector correlations, so specialising in one sector concentrates exposures that tend to default together.
cards.originalText: Intrasector default correlations are typically LOWER than intersector correlations, so the lender should specialise in a single sector.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: Default correlations are approximately equal within and across sectors, so the composition of the portfolio by sector is not a useful lever.
cards.explanation: Intrasector default correlations are well documented to be higher than intersector ones, which is the basis for sector concentration limits in credit portfolio management.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk
cards.reading: Meissner, Correlation Risk
cards.statement: When a bank reduces the concentration ratio of its loan portfolio and the default correlation between the loans is strictly less than one, the joint probability of default is most likely to decrease.
cards.explanation: With default correlation below one, spreading exposure across more names reduces the probability that exposures default together. Only at a correlation of one do obligors default as a block, leaving joint default risk unchanged.
cards.originalText: It will decrease.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Under age-weighted historical simulation, more recent observations are weighted more heavily and distant observations less heavily.
cards.explanation: Age-weighted historical simulation gives observations geometrically declining weights according to their age, controlled by a decay parameter between 0 and 1.
cards.originalText: More recent observations are weighted more heavily and distant observations less heavily.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Under age-weighted historical simulation, all observations in the window are weighted equally.
cards.explanation: Equal weighting of all observations is basic historical simulation. Age weighting gives recent observations more weight and older ones geometrically less.
cards.originalText: All observations in the window are weighted equally.
cards.correction: Under basic historical simulation, all observations in the window are weighted equally.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Under basic historical simulation, all observations in the window are weighted equally.
cards.explanation: Equal weighting of all observations is basic historical simulation. Age weighting gives recent observations more weight and older ones geometrically less.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Under age-weighted historical simulation, the decay parameter takes a value of 1.
cards.explanation: A decay parameter of exactly 1 removes all decay and collapses the method back to basic, equally weighted historical simulation. The decay parameter lies between 0 and 1.
cards.originalText: The decay parameter takes a value of 1.
cards.correction: Under age-weighted historical simulation, the decay parameter takes a value between 0 and 1.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Under age-weighted historical simulation, the decay parameter takes a value between 0 and 1.
cards.explanation: A decay parameter of exactly 1 removes all decay and collapses the method back to basic, equally weighted historical simulation. The decay parameter lies between 0 and 1.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Under age-weighted historical simulation, the historical window of observations must not exceed 250 days.
cards.explanation: Age-weighted historical simulation prescribes no window length; it is defined by geometrically declining weights on older observations.
cards.originalText: The historical window of observations must not exceed 250 days.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Volatility-weighted historical simulation, the Hull and White approach, discards every historical return drawn from a period whose volatility differed materially from today's, shortening the effective window.
cards.explanation: Volatility-weighted historical simulation retains every observation and rescales it by a volatility ratio; nothing is discarded.
cards.originalText: It discards every historical return drawn from a period whose volatility differed materially from today's, shortening the effective window.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Volatility-weighted historical simulation, the Hull and White approach, rescales each historical return by the ratio of today's volatility forecast to the volatility that prevailed on the day the return was observed, so the adjusted series reflects current market conditions.
cards.explanation: The Hull and White adjustment multiplies each historical return by the current volatility forecast divided by the volatility at the time of the observation, putting all returns on today's volatility scale.
cards.originalText: It rescales each historical return by the ratio of today's volatility forecast to the volatility that prevailed on the day the return was observed, so the adjusted series reflects current market conditions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Volatility-weighted historical simulation, the Hull and White approach, rescales each historical return by the ratio of the volatility that prevailed when the return was observed to today's volatility forecast, so that quiet periods are amplified.
cards.explanation: The ratio is today's volatility forecast divided by the historical volatility, so returns are scaled up when today is more volatile than when they were observed.
cards.originalText: It rescales each historical return by the ratio of the volatility that prevailed when the return was observed to today's volatility forecast, so that quiet periods are amplified.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Volatility-weighted historical simulation, the Hull and White approach, assigns geometrically declining weights by age, on the grounds that volatility is higher in recent data.
cards.explanation: Geometrically declining weights by age describe age-weighted historical simulation. Volatility weighting instead rescales each return by the ratio of current to historical volatility.
cards.originalText: It assigns geometrically declining weights by age, on the grounds that volatility is higher in recent data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A correlation-weighted approach within historical simulation forces all pairwise asset correlations to zero by partitioning returns into uncorrelated blocks, while leaving individual volatilities unchanged.
cards.explanation: Correlation weighting imposes a target correlation matrix, which is generally not zero. Forcing correlations to zero would destroy the dependence structure and the diversification effects.
cards.originalText: It forces all pairwise asset correlations to zero by partitioning returns into uncorrelated blocks, while leaving individual volatilities unchanged.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A correlation-weighted approach within historical simulation imposes a desired set of updated correlations among assets by systematically adjusting historical returns, typically without altering each asset's own volatility.
cards.explanation: Correlation-weighted historical simulation transforms historical returns (for example via Cholesky decompositions) so they exhibit a target correlation matrix, while leaving each asset's own volatility unchanged.
cards.originalText: It imposes a desired set of updated correlations among assets by systematically adjusting historical returns, typically without altering each asset's own volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk

cards.statement: A correlation-weighted approach within historical simulation re-weights observed co-movements so that the sample correlation matrix becomes diagonal, leaving only variances.
cards.explanation: Making the correlation matrix diagonal is the zero-correlation case. Correlation weighting imposes a target (generally non-zero) correlation structure.
cards.originalText: It re-weights observed co-movements so that the sample correlation matrix becomes diagonal, leaving only variances.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: A correlation-weighted approach within historical simulation replicates only those return paths whose correlations exceed a specified threshold and discards the rest.
cards.explanation: Correlation weighting adjusts all historical returns to exhibit target correlations; discarding paths would shrink the sample and introduce selection bias.
cards.originalText: It replicates only those return paths whose correlations exceed a specified threshold and discards the rest.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Filtered historical simulation fits a time-varying volatility model such as GARCH, standardises historical returns by the fitted conditional volatility, and then resamples the standardised residuals before rescaling to current volatility.
cards.explanation: Filtered historical simulation models volatility (typically with GARCH), standardises returns by conditional volatility to get roughly i.i.d. residuals, bootstraps those residuals, and rescales them to current volatility.
cards.originalText: It fits a time-varying volatility model such as GARCH, standardises historical returns by the fitted conditional volatility, and then resamples the standardised residuals before rescaling to current volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Filtered historical simulation reorders past returns chronologically to match short-term volatility changes but leaves the correlation structure unaltered.
cards.explanation: Filtered historical simulation standardises returns by GARCH conditional volatility, bootstraps the residuals and rescales to current volatility. Historical simulation is invariant to the order of the sample, so reordering returns achieves nothing.
cards.originalText: It reorders past returns chronologically to match short-term volatility changes but leaves the correlation structure unaltered.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare age-, volatility-, correlation-weighted and filtered historical simulation
cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Filtered historical simulation discards all returns falling outside a user-defined confidence interval, ensuring the final distribution contains no extreme tail events.
cards.explanation: Filtered historical simulation is designed to represent extreme events better, and it can generate losses larger than any in the raw sample.
cards.originalText: It discards all returns falling outside a user-defined confidence interval, ensuring the final distribution contains no extreme tail events.

cards.subject: Market Risk

cards.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
cards.statement: Filtered historical simulation transforms each asset's average return to zero while holding the standard deviation fixed at its historical level.
cards.explanation: Filtered historical simulation standardises returns by their fitted conditional volatility and rescales to current volatility; it relaxes, rather than imposes, a fixed historical standard deviation.
cards.originalText: It transforms each asset's average return to zero while holding the standard deviation fixed at its historical level.

cards.statement: Age weighting and volatility weighting both leave the effective sample size unchanged, whereas correlation weighting reduces it.
cards.explanation: Age weighting concentrates weight on recent observations and so shrinks the effective sample size; correlation weighting retains all observations at full weight and only adjusts their dependence structure.

cards.loText: Describe a regression hedge and how it improves a DV01-neutral hedge

cards.statement: In a regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument is derived from the slope coefficient of a historical yield regression.
cards.explanation: A regression hedge multiplies the DV01 hedge ratio by beta, the slope from regressing changes in the hedged bond's yield on changes in the hedging instrument's yield. The DV01-neutral hedge is the special case beta equals one.

cards.reading: Empirical Approaches to Risk Metrics and Hedging
cards.statement: In a regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument adjusts dynamically according to forecasts of market sentiment.
cards.explanation: Regression hedging is backward looking: the risk weight is the slope coefficient estimated from historical yield changes, not a forecast of market sentiment.

cards.statement: Level regression models absolute levels and captures long-run relationships, while change regression models first differences and reduces the risk of spurious correlation from non-stationary data.

cards.statement: A regression hedge and a reverse regression hedge use identical calculations and therefore produce identical hedge ratios.
cards.explanation: A regression and a reverse regression give reciprocal slopes only when R-squared equals 1. In general the product of the two slopes equals R-squared, so the hedge ratios differ.

cards.statement: A regression hedge and a reverse regression hedge produce different hedge ratios because the choice of which yield is the independent variable determines the direction in which sensitivity is measured, and the two slopes are not reciprocals of one another unless the fit is perfect.
cards.explanation: Least squares minimises errors in the dependent variable only, so regressing in each direction minimises different quantities. The product of the two slopes equals R-squared, so they are reciprocals only when the fit is perfect.

cards.loText: Describe PCA and explain its application to constructing a hedging portfolio

cards.statement: Applying PCA to hedge construction means calculating the portfolio's sensitivities to the dominant principal components, then taking hedging positions that neutralise those sensitivities.
cards.explanation: A PCA hedge decomposes historical yield changes into principal components, measures the portfolio's sensitivity to each dominant component, and takes offsetting positions to neutralise them.
cards.originalText: Calculate the portfolio's sensitivities to the dominant principal components, then take hedging positions that neutralise those sensitivities.

cards.loText: Describe PCA and explain its application to constructing a hedging portfolio

cards.statement: When PCA is applied to historical changes in a government yield curve, the first three components typically correspond to LEVEL, SLOPE and CURVATURE, they are uncorrelated with one another by construction, and the first alone usually explains the large majority of the total variance.
cards.explanation: Yield curve principal components are typically level, slope and curvature. They are orthogonal by construction and ordered by variance explained, with the level factor usually dominant.

cards.reading: Extreme Value Theory
cards.statement: Extreme events rarely carry warning signs, so markets cannot prepare for them in any way.
cards.explanation: Some extreme events do carry warning signs. The concern is their severity and the unpredictability of their timing, not a total absence of signals.

cards.reading: Extreme Value Theory
cards.statement: Extreme events are typically very costly and can create a ripple effect across the global market.
cards.explanation: Risk reflects probability weighted by severity. Extreme events have tiny probabilities but very large, contagious impacts, so their expected impact can be substantial and can threaten an institution's survival.

cards.reading: Extreme Value Theory
cards.statement: The primary difficulty in modelling extreme events is that there are very few historical observations from which a credible model can be built.
cards.explanation: Extreme events are rare, so there are few observations and tail estimates have very wide confidence intervals. This is why a parametric tail model such as EVT is needed.
cards.originalText: There are very few historical observations from which a credible model can be built.

cards.loText: Describe EVT and its use in risk management
cards.reading: Extreme Value Theory
cards.statement: Extreme values do not conform to any established loss distribution.

cards.statement: Extreme events are best modelled through the application of the central limit theorem.
